blogs.title: Fraudulent‑Inducement Meets TikTok: How the Fifth Circuit Re‑configures Securities Fraud for Influencers
blogs.description: This post examines the court’s application of the fraudulent‑inducement theory—declaring that social‑media fitness and finance gurus can be prosecuted under §1348 for deceitfully steering followers into buying securities. It traces the line from classic mail‑and‑wire fraud to today’s algorithm‑driven marketplaces and explores why the "right‑to‑control" rationale rejected in Ciminelli no longer applies on the pulse of influencer culture.

blogs.title: Busting the ‘Lost‑Information’ Defense: Why Deprivation of Economic Insight Isn’t Enough to Avoid Securities Fraud
blogs.description: Here we dissect the Fifth Circuit’s rebuttal to the district court’s right‑to‑control theory, linking it to the Supreme Court’s holding in Kousisis. By breaking down the distinction between traditional property interests and the valuable economic information that followers trust, the piece clarifies the modern threshold for a securities‑fraud “scheme to defraud” and shows how the court’s analysis affirms that mere financial deception suffices.

blogs.title: Indictment Sufficiency on Trial: What United States v. Constantinescu Means for Prosecutorial Drafting
blogs.description: Focusing on the procedural side, this analysis reviews the de‑novo sufficiency standard, the repetition of elemental requirements, and the Fifth Circuit’s emphasis on enumerated offenses. It will explain how the court’s decision informs prosecutors drafting indictments that must withstand a quick dismissal by lower courts, especially in complex white‑collar cases involving online platforms.

blogs.title: From Pump‑and‑Dump to Platform‑Policy: How the Fifth Circuit’s Ruling Shapes Future Regulations for Online Influencers
blogs.description: Looking ahead, this post evaluates how the ruling signals a trend toward treating influencer‑driven market manipulation as outright securities fraud. It discusses potential legislative and self‑regulatory responses, the role of platform accountability, and the evolving intersection between securities law, fraud statutes, and digital media governance.
